The rain had been falling for three days, not hard, but with the kind of persistence that makes the world feel slightly thinner. I stood under the awning of a closed bookstore and watched the street fill with reflections. Cars passed like slow thoughts. A woman in a yellow coat hurried by, holding a paper bag against her chest as if it contained something that might dissolve.

I have always liked the hour just before a city decides what it is going to be. Not morning, not night—something in between, when the lights are on but the intentions are still soft. In that hour the ordinary things look briefly invented: the way a puddle holds an entire traffic light, the way steam rises from a grate and vanishes into the same air that carries the smell of bread from somewhere I couldn’t see.

Someone once told me that attention is a form of generosity. I didn’t understand it then. I thought generosity required giving something away—time, money, effort. But standing there, doing nothing useful, I felt how much of the world is simply waiting to be noticed without being used. The yellow coat disappeared around the corner. The puddle kept the red light a moment longer than the signal itself. A single leaf, already brown, spun once in the gutter and stuck.

I thought about how most of what we call meaning arrives sideways. We plan the important conversations and then the real sentence happens while we’re looking for our keys. We study the map and miss the turn that would have shown us the river. The rain kept its own slow count. I stayed until the bookstore lights clicked off behind the glass, one by one, and the reflections grew darker and more precise.

When I finally stepped out, the water was cold against my ankles. I didn’t mind. For a little while the street and I were made of the same temporary thing—motion, weather, and the small decision to keep walking anyway.
